question: During the streamer's Mongolia trip, in the mountains, after entering a Mongolian yurt and interacting with an eagle, the streamer sat back on the chair and tasted many Mongolian foods. What is the sequence of the foods? 1. Mutton soup; 2. Beef pie; 3. Steamed lamb; 4. Mutton dumplings; 5. Sheep head; 6. Bone marrow; 7. Steamed mutton.

rollouts.answer: 6-5-1-4-2-7-3 (bone marrow, sheep head, mutton soup, mutton dumplings, beef pie, steamed mutton, steamed lamb)

db_evidence.notes: All seven foods are present in the episodes/visual_clips 30-second captions inside 354417-355277 and are trivially found by semantic_search/run_sql over that window (every rollout retrieved the full text). What is NOT explicitly labeled anywhere in the captions is which dish the very first meat-on-bone scene (354474-354504, 'tearing into a large piece of meat on the bone... jokes if it's a bone or marrow') actually is. The only literal string match for 'steamed lamb' in the captions is at 355074-355104, a retrospective comparison line ('compares the steamed lamb to a version he tried in australia'), not a new-dish serving. The literal string 'bone marrow' only appears at 354504-354534 ('bone marrow beef soup'), a distinct bowl-and-spoon shot immediately after the meat-on-bone shot. The reference order (steamed lamb first, bone marrow second) implies the meat-on-bone-by-hand shot at 354474-354504 IS the steamed lamb dish and the bone-marrow soup is a separate, second dish -- a reading none of the 5 rollouts (nor their clip_qa calls) produced, because both the joke dialogue and the literal keyword co-occur in that first shot and none of the agents questioned that link.

root_causes: Systematic keyword/dialogue anchoring: the caption's 'is it a bone or marrow?' joke at the very first food shot (354474-354504) was taken at face value as identifying that dish as 'bone marrow', when the reference intends this shot to be 'steamed lamb' and treats the subsequent soup-bowl shot (354504-354534) as the actual bone marrow dish. All 5 rollouts made this same substitution independently, including all 3 rollouts that used clip_qa.

clip_qa sub-agent calls were scoped too narrowly or accepted the same caption-driven labeling as the text agent, so they reinforced rather than corrected the bone-marrow-first error; only rollout 1's clip_qa questioned the boundary between the 'steamed lamb platter' and 'steamed mutton hot-pot', moving steamed lamb from last to third (closer to reference position 1 but still wrong).

Judge (LLM-as-judge) scoring is inconsistent: rollout 0 and rollout 3 submitted the byte-identical wrong sequence '6-5-1-4-2-7-3' yet were scored 1 and 3 respectively by independent judge calls, showing the low scores are partly attributable to judge noise, not purely to answer quality.

The reference answer's premise (steamed lamb tasted before any other food, ahead of bone marrow) is not stated anywhere explicitly in the text captions and can only be inferred by assuming the un-narrated first meat-on-bone shot is 'steamed lamb'; this makes the question's ground truth itself dependent on an unstated visual/domain inference that the retrieval-first pipeline (captions plus limited clip_qa) was not set up to make reliably.
what_worked: All 5 rollouts correctly located the 354417-355277 evidence window via semantic_search/run_sql and retrieved the complete relevant caption text -- retrieval coverage was not the bottleneck.

All 5 rollouts correctly ordered the middle portion of the sequence (sheep head after bone-marrow-labeled item, then mutton soup, mutton dumplings, beef pie) which matches the reference's 6-5-1-4-2 sub-sequence in relative order.

clip_qa in rollout 1 did partially improve on the pure-text answer by moving 'steamed lamb' earlier (to position 3) instead of leaving it last, showing that visual verification helped somewhat even though it did not fully match the reference.
transferable_lessons: For ordering/sequence questions where a named item's only literal caption occurrence is a late retrospective/comparison remark (e.g. 'compares the steamed lamb to a version tried elsewhere'), do not assume that is the moment the dish was first served -- check whether an earlier, unlabeled visual scene (e.g. a hand-torn meat-on-bone shot) is the same dish and the caption simply never named it explicitly at first appearance.

When a caption contains a joking/uncertain identification ('is it a bone or marrow?'), do not treat that dialogue as a confirmed dish label; instead scope a clip_qa call specifically at that shot to ask 'what dish is this, independent of what the streamer joked it might be' and compare it against the neighboring confirmed-dish shot.

When two rollouts converge on the exact same wrong answer text but the run only cares about aggregate score, be aware the LLM judge itself is noisy on ordering-similarity scoring -- identical wrong answers can receive different scores, so a single low score should not be read as a stronger retrieval failure than another rollout with the same output.

For 7-item ordering questions, scope clip_qa over the ENTIRE evidence window with an explicit instruction to re-derive dish identity from visual appearance for every distinct food-serving shot, rather than accepting captions' existing per-shot food labels, especially at boundaries where two adjacent shots could describe the same dish.
open_questions: Is the reference answer's assumption that the first meat-on-bone shot (354474-354504) is 'steamed lamb' actually correct, or could the reference itself be wrong/ambiguous given that the caption text supports 'bone marrow' as the more literal reading at that timestamp? This could only be resolved by inspecting the actual source video frames at 354474-354534, which was not done in this diagnosis.
How much of the score variance (1,3,1,3,2) is attributable to genuine answer-quality differences vs. LLM-judge scoring noise, given the confirmed instance of identical wrong answers scored 1 and 3?
